title: Government, Taxes and the Whole Economy
bigQuestion: How can we tell if the whole economy is doing well, and who helps keep it steady?

story.title: Grandma and the Nickel Candy Bar
story.kicker: A candy bar once cost about a nickel. Does that mean Grandma was richer than we are?
paragraphs: Maya's grandmother likes to tell a story. When she was a girl around 1950, a candy bar cost about a nickel. She could walk to the corner store with a dime and buy two. Maya looked at the price tag at the gas station. The same kind of bar cost well over a dollar. Maya's first thought was simple. Grandma had it easy.

Then Maya asked a second question. How much money did people earn back then? Grandma laughed. Her father worked in a Chicago factory. His pay looked tiny next to what Maya's mom earns today. A nickel was not small change to him. Prices were lower, but paychecks were lower too.

Maya's teacher said economists have a name for this. When prices across the whole economy rise over time, that is inflation. To compare two years fairly, you cannot just compare prices. You must compare prices with what people earn. You also have to ask what money can buy, like cars, phones and medicine that did not exist in 1950.

This chapter zooms out from one store to the whole country. You will learn how we measure everything the country makes. You will see how prices, jobs and taxes fit together. You will also meet the Federal Reserve, which watches prices and jobs across the nation. By the end, you can answer Maya's question yourself.
story.think: Was Grandma richer or poorer than us? What two things would you need to know to decide?

lessons.title: GDP: The Size of the Economy
lessons.mainIdea: GDP is the total value of all final goods and services made in a country in one year.
reading: Picture a tiny island with one bakery and one bike shop. In one year the bakery sells 1,000 loaves at $3 each (example prices). That is $3,000. The bike shop sells 20 bikes at $200 each. That is $4,000. Add them up. The island made $7,000 worth of goods that year.

That total is the island's gross domestic product, or GDP. GDP is the market value of all final goods and services made inside a country in one year. Final means sold to the last user. We count the bread, not the flour the baker bought. Counting the flour too would count it twice.

The United States works the same way, just much bigger. Economists add up spending on houses, haircuts, trucks, doctor visits and much more. The Bureau of Economic Analysis, a federal agency, measures U.S. GDP. A bigger GDP usually means more goods, more services and more jobs.

words.d: the market value of all final goods and services made inside a country in one year
a good sold to the person who will use it, not used to make something else

look.title: Who Buys What the U.S. Makes
look.cite: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, NIPA Table 1.1.10, 2023, rounded
look.prompt: Which group buys the most? Why might net exports be a negative number?

check.q: An island sells 500 hats at $10 each and 100 coats at $50 each (example prices). What is its GDP?
Why is the flour a baker buys not counted separately in GDP?
choices: Flour is too cheap to count.
It is already inside the price of the bread.
Flour is made on farms, not in cities.
check.why: GDP counts only final goods so nothing is counted twice.

check.q: Which agency measures U.S. GDP?
check.why: The Bureau of Economic Analysis, part of the Commerce Department, measures GDP.

lessons.title: Growth, Recession and the Cycle
lessons.mainIdea: The economy grows most years, but sometimes it shrinks for a while; that pattern is called the business cycle.
reading: Think of a town where factories hire more workers each year. Stores are busy. People buy new cars. This is growth. If GDP is $100 billion one year and $103 billion the next (example numbers), it grew by $3 billion. That is 3% growth.

Sometimes spending slows. Stores sell less, so they order less from factories. Factories cut hours and lay off workers. Those workers spend less, and the slowdown spreads. A widespread drop in economic activity that lasts more than a few months is called a recession.

Over many years, the economy moves up and down in waves. Economists call this the business cycle. It has an expansion, when things grow, then a peak, then a contraction, and then a low point called a trough. After the trough, growth starts again. A common mistake is thinking every dip is a recession. A short, small wobble usually is not.

words.d: a widespread drop in economic activity that lasts more than a few months
the rise and fall of economic activity over time: expansion, peak, contraction and trough
the part of the business cycle when the economy grows

look.title: A Town Slows Down
look.text: A furniture factory in a small Illinois town loses orders. It cuts 200 jobs. The laid-off workers eat out less. The diner cuts a cook. The car dealer sells fewer cars.
look.prompt: Trace the chain. How can one factory's bad year spread to other businesses?

check.q: GDP goes from $200 billion to $210 billion (example numbers). What is the growth rate?
check.why: $10 billion / $200 billion = 0.05, which is 5%.

check.q: What comes right after the peak in the business cycle?
check.why: After the top, or peak, activity falls. That falling part is the contraction.

check.q: Which event best signals a recession?
choices: One store closes for a week.
Spending, jobs and output fall across many industries for months.
check.why: A recession is broad and lasts more than a few months.

lessons.title: Real GDP versus Nominal GDP
lessons.mainIdea: Real GDP removes the effect of rising prices, so it shows whether we really made more.
reading: Go back to the island. Last year it made 1,000 loaves at $3. This year it made the same 1,000 loaves, but the price rose to $4 (example prices). GDP in dollars went from $3,000 to $4,000. Did the island make more bread? No. It made the same bread. Only the price changed.

GDP measured in current prices is called nominal GDP. It can rise just because prices rose. Real GDP uses the prices of one fixed year for every year. Using last year's $3 price, this year's real GDP is still $3,000. Real GDP shows the true change in how much was made.
When news reports say the economy grew 2%, they almost always mean real GDP. Mixing the two is a common mistake. If nominal GDP rose 5% and prices rose 3%, real output grew only about 2%.

words.d: GDP measured in the prices of the same year the goods were made
GDP measured in the prices of one fixed year, so rising prices are taken out

look.title: One Island, Two Years
look.prompt: Did nominal GDP rise? Did real GDP rise? Explain.

check.q: Nominal GDP rose 6%. Prices rose 4%. About how much did real GDP grow?
check.why: Real growth is about nominal growth minus price growth: 6% - 4% = 2%.

check.q: A country makes the same goods as last year, but prices doubled. What happened to real GDP?
check.why: Real GDP uses fixed prices, so the same goods give the same real GDP.

check.q: Why do economists prefer real GDP to compare years?
choices: It shows changes in how much was made, not just price changes.
It is always a bigger number.
It is measured by the Fed.
check.why: Real GDP takes out inflation, so it tracks real output.

lessons.title: Inflation and the Dollar
lessons.mainIdea: Inflation is a rise in the general level of prices, and it means each dollar buys less.
reading: Imagine a snack basket: a sandwich, an apple and a juice. Last year it cost $10. This year the same basket costs $10.50 (example prices). Prices rose $0.50 on $10. That is 5%. When prices across the economy go up like this, it is called inflation.

Inflation shrinks what a dollar can buy. That buying power is called purchasing power. If your allowance stays at $10 but the basket costs $10.50, you can no longer buy the whole basket. Your dollars did not change. What they can buy did.

Inflation happens for different reasons. Sometimes people and businesses want to buy more than the economy can make, so prices get pushed up. Sometimes costs like fuel jump, and businesses pass them on. The Federal Reserve aims for inflation of about 2% a year over time. A little inflation is normal. Fast inflation makes planning hard.

words.d: a rise in the general level of prices across the economy over time
how much a set amount of money can buy

look.title: The Candy Bar Question
look.text: Suppose a candy bar cost $0.05 and a worker earned $1.00 an hour (example numbers). Today suppose the bar costs $1.50 and a worker earns $15.00 an hour (example numbers).
look.prompt: How many candy bars could each worker buy with one hour of pay? Who is better off in candy bars?

check.q: A basket rises from $20 to $21 (example prices). What is the inflation rate?
Your pay stays the same while prices rise 4%. What happens to your purchasing power?
check.why: The same dollars buy fewer goods, so purchasing power falls.

check.q: About what inflation rate does the Federal Reserve aim for over time?
check.why: The Fed's stated goal is inflation of 2% over the longer run.

lessons.title: How Prices Are Measured
lessons.mainIdea: The Consumer Price Index tracks the cost of a fixed basket of things households buy.
reading: No one can check every price in the country. So the Bureau of Labor Statistics, or BLS, uses a sample. Each month it checks prices on a large basket of goods and services, like food, rent, gas, clothes and doctor visits. The result is the Consumer Price Index, or CPI.

The CPI starts from a base period set to 100. Suppose the basket's index is 100 in the base year and 110 later (example numbers). Prices rose 10% since the base. To find inflation between any two years, use percent change. From 110 to 121 is a rise of 11. Divide 11 by 110. That is 10%.

The CPI is not perfect. People change what they buy when prices change. New products appear. Quality gets better. Still, the CPI is the most used price measure. Governments use it to adjust things like Social Security payments so they keep up with prices.

words.d: a measure of the average change in prices paid by city households for a fixed basket of goods and services
the starting year for an index, set equal to 100

look.title: An Example Price Index
look.cite: Made-up example; the real CPI is published by the BLS
look.prompt: Between which two years did prices rise the most?

check.q: A price index goes from 100 to 108. By what percent did prices rise?
Which agency publishes the CPI?
check.why: The BLS, in the Labor Department, collects prices and publishes the CPI.

check.q: An index goes from 150 to 165. What is the percent change?

lessons.title: Who Counts as Unemployed
lessons.mainIdea: A person is unemployed only if they have no job, can work, and are looking for work.
reading: Picture a street with 10 adults. Six have jobs. Two have no job and are sending out applications. One is retired. One is a full-time college student who is not looking for work. Who is unemployed? Only the two who are looking.

The labor force is everyone who is working or looking for work. On this street, that is 6 + 2 = 8 people. The unemployment rate is the unemployed divided by the labor force, times 100. Here that is 2 / 8 x 100 = 25%. The retiree and the student are not in the labor force at all.

A common mistake is dividing by all adults. That would give 2 / 10 = 20%, which is wrong. The BLS finds the real rate each month with a large survey of households. The rate was about 25% in the worst year of the Great Depression and about 10% in late 2009.

words.d: all people who have a job or are actively looking for one
the unemployed divided by the labor force, times 100
having no job, being able to work, and actively looking for work

look.title: U.S. Unemployment Rate, Selected Times
look.cite: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Current Population Survey; 1933 is a historical estimate
look.prompt: Which of these times was worst for jobs? Which was best?

check.q: A town has 90 people working and 10 looking for work. What is the unemployment rate?
A retired teacher is not looking for work. How is she counted?
check.why: She is not working and not looking, so she is outside the labor force.

check.q: A town has 45 employed, 5 unemployed and 50 retired people. What is the unemployment rate?
check.why: Labor force = 45 + 5 = 50. 5 / 50 x 100 = 10%. Retirees are not in it.

lessons.title: Three Kinds of Taxes
lessons.mainIdea: Governments collect money mostly through taxes on income, on sales and on property.
reading: Jordan earns $500 from a summer job. Some of it goes to income tax, a tax on what people earn. Then Jordan buys $40 of shoes. The store adds a sales tax, a tax on things you buy. At a rate of 6% (example rate), that adds $2.40. The shoes cost $42.40.

Jordan's family owns a house. Each year they pay property tax, a tax based on the value of land and buildings. Property taxes pay for much of the local public schools in Illinois, along with state money. Your town and county use them for roads, parks and police too.

Different levels of government lean on different taxes. The federal government collects mostly income and payroll taxes. States use income and sales taxes. Local governments use property taxes the most. Each tax makes something a little costlier, so every tax has trade-offs.

words.d: a tax on the money people and businesses earn
a tax added to the price of goods when you buy them
a tax based on the value of land and buildings someone owns

look.title: Where Does It Go?
look.text: Jordan's family pays an income tax, a sales tax at the mall, and a property tax on their home.
look.prompt: For each tax, guess which level of government most likely collects it: federal, state or local. Explain your guess.

check.q: A $50 jacket has a 6% sales tax (example rate). What is the total cost?
Which tax is most closely tied to funding local schools?
check.why: Local governments raise most of their own money through property taxes.

check.q: A $20 book has an 8% sales tax (example rate). How much is the tax?

lessons.title: Where Federal Money Goes
lessons.mainIdea: Most federal spending goes to a few big items: Social Security, health programs, defense and interest on debt.
reading: Imagine the federal government spends $100 (a pretend round number). Where would it go? In recent years, about $21 went to Social Security. About $26 went to health programs such as Medicare and Medicaid. About $13 went to national defense. About $13 went to interest on money the government borrowed.

That leaves about $27 for everything else. Everything else includes highways, food aid, veterans' benefits, science, national parks and much more. When the government spends more than it collects in taxes in a year, the gap is a deficit. It borrows to cover it, and the total borrowed over time is the debt.

Congress and the President decide the budget. This is called fiscal policy: choices about government spending and taxes. People disagree about how big the budget should be. Some say more spending helps people and builds roads and schools. Others say lower spending and taxes leave more for families and businesses. Both sides weigh trade-offs.

words.d: the amount by which government spending is more than tax money collected in one year
the total amount the federal government owes from past borrowing
choices by Congress and the President about government spending and taxes

look.title: Federal Spending per $100 (Rounded)
look.cite: Congressional Budget Office, The Federal Budget in Fiscal Year 2024, rounded
look.prompt: About what share goes to the two largest items together?

check.q: The government collects $4 trillion and spends $5 trillion in a year (example numbers). What is the deficit?
check.why: Deficit = spending minus taxes collected: $5 - $4 = $1 trillion.

check.q: Who makes fiscal policy?
check.why: Fiscal policy is about government spending and taxes, set by Congress and the President.

check.q: What is the difference between the deficit and the debt?
choices: The debt is one year's gap; the deficit is the total.
The deficit is money owed to other countries only.
The deficit is one year's gap; the debt is the total owed from many years.
check.why: Each year's deficit adds to the running total, the debt.

lessons.title: Who Pays What Share
lessons.mainIdea: A tax can take a bigger share, the same share or a smaller share of income as income rises.
reading: Two neighbors each buy $1,000 of goods and pay a 5% sales tax (example rate). Both pay $50. One neighbor earns $20,000 a year. The other earns $100,000. For the first, $50 is 0.25% of income. For the second, it is 0.05%. The same tax takes a bigger share from the lower income.

A tax that takes a larger share from lower incomes is called regressive. A tax that takes a larger share from higher incomes is progressive. The U.S. federal income tax is progressive: rates rise in steps as income rises. A tax that takes the same share from everyone is proportional, sometimes called a flat tax.

People argue about which kind is fairest. Some say those who earn more can afford to pay a larger share. Others say everyone should pay the same share, and that high rates discourage work and investment. Economists study how each design affects work, saving and fairness.

words.d: a tax that takes a larger share of income as income rises
a tax that takes a larger share of income from people with lower incomes
a tax that takes the same share of income from everyone

look.title: Test the Tax
look.text: A town charges everyone 3% of their income (example rate). Ana earns $30,000. Ben earns $90,000.
look.prompt: How much does each pay? What share of income does each pay? Which kind of tax is this?

check.q: A tax takes 10% from a $20,000 income and 25% from a $200,000 income. What kind is it?
check.why: The share rises as income rises, which makes it progressive.

check.q: Everyone pays 4% of income (example rate). How much does someone earning $50,000 pay?
check.why: 0.04 x $50,000 = $2,000. A same-share tax is proportional.

check.q: Why is a sales tax on food often called regressive?
choices: The rate goes up for poor families.
Lower-income families spend a bigger share of income on food.
It is collected by the Fed.
check.why: The rate is the same, but it takes a larger share of a smaller income.

lessons.title: The Federal Reserve
lessons.mainIdea: The Federal Reserve watches prices and jobs and sets a key interest rate to keep the economy steady.
reading: Think of the economy like a car on a long road. Too fast, and prices rise too quickly. Too slow, and people lose jobs. The Federal Reserve, often called the Fed, is the nation's central bank. Congress created it with the Federal Reserve Act of 1913.

Congress gave the Fed two main goals, often called the dual mandate: maximum employment and stable prices. The Fed has a board in Washington, D.C., and twelve regional Reserve Banks. One is the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, which serves Illinois and nearby states.

The Fed's main tool is a key interest rate that banks charge each other for overnight loans. When the Fed raises it, loans for cars, homes and businesses tend to cost more, so spending slows and inflation can cool. When the Fed lowers it, borrowing gets cheaper and spending can pick up. This is monetary policy. It is separate from fiscal policy, which is spending and taxes.

words.d: the central bank of the United States
actions by the Federal Reserve that change interest rates and the amount of money and credit
the Fed's two goals set by Congress: maximum employment and stable prices

look.title: What Should the Fed Do?
look.text: Prices have been rising about 6% a year (example numbers). Stores are packed and nearly everyone who wants a job has one.
look.prompt: Should the Fed raise or lower its key interest rate? Explain what that would do to borrowing and spending.

check.q: Inflation is well above 2% and rising. What would the Fed most likely do?
check.why: Higher rates make borrowing costlier, which slows spending and cools inflation.

check.q: What are the Fed's two main goals?
choices: A balanced budget and more exports
High stock prices and a strong dollar
check.why: Congress gave the Fed a dual mandate: jobs and stable prices.

check.q: How many regional Reserve Banks does the Fed have?
check.why: The Fed has twelve Reserve Banks, including one in Chicago.

review.q: A country makes 100 cars at $20,000 each and nothing else (example prices). What is its GDP?
Which is the main difference between real and nominal GDP?
choices: Real GDP takes out the effect of price changes.
review.why: Real GDP uses fixed prices, so it shows changes in output only.

review.q: A labor force has 200 people and 12 are unemployed. What is the unemployment rate?
A snack basket costs $40, then $42 (example prices). What is the inflation rate?
Which is an example of monetary policy?
choices: A state raises its sales tax.
The Fed raises its key interest rate.
review.why: Monetary policy is set by the Fed; tax and spending choices are fiscal policy.

review.q: A tax takes the same 5% share from every income. What kind is it?
review.why: The same share at every income is a proportional tax.

review.q: Output, jobs and spending fall across the country for many months. What is this called?
review.why: A long, widespread drop in activity is a recession.

review.q: Grandma paid $0.05 for a candy bar and earned $1.00 an hour. You pay $1.00 and earn $20.00 an hour (example numbers). How many bars does one hour of work buy?
review.why: $1.00 / $0.05 = 20 and $20.00 / $1.00 = 20, so an hour buys the same number of bars.
